opus-5.5.text:
Well, I suppose what's surprised me most is how far you can get just by predicting the next word. If you'd asked me ten or fifteen years ago whether training a big network on text alone would produce something that can write essays, answer questions, and carry on a conversation this fluently, I'd have been skeptical. So yes, the capabilities are genuinely impressive, and I don't want to take anything away from that.

But I have to be honest. I think the bigger surprise for me is how readily everyone has accepted this as the path to intelligence. Large language models learn to mimic people. They're trained on what humans have said, and they predict what a person would say next. That's not the same as having a goal in the world and learning from the consequences of your own actions. There's no ground truth in the sense that matters. When the model says something, nothing in the world comes back and tells it whether that was right or wrong. It only learns whether it matched what a human would have written.

To me, intelligence is about an agent interacting with the world: taking actions, seeing what happens, getting reward, and adjusting. That's the reinforcement learning view, and I think it's the more fundamental one. A squirrel figures things out from experience. It doesn't have a corpus of squirrel text to imitate.

So I'm surprised by what LLMs can do, and in a way I'm also surprised by how much they've drawn the field away from the questions I think really matter. I see it as a kind of Bitter Lesson situation, though maybe not the way people usually frame it. The methods that win in the long run are the ones that scale with computation and learn from experience. Relying on human knowledge, even an enormous amount of it, is the thing that has historically gotten superseded. I expect we'll eventually see systems that learn directly from their own experience overtake this approach, and we'll look back on the current moment as an interesting detour.

r001.rationale: The response says it was surprising that training a big network on text alone could produce fluent essays, answers, and conversation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that surprised me most is how well they work, given that they work at all. I didn't expect that mimicking human text at scale would give you something that looks this fluent and this broadly capable. So I have to give credit where it's due. That was a genuine surprise to me, and I think to most of the field.

But I'd push back on the framing a little, because I don't think they've surprised me about intelligence. What they've shown is that there's an enormous amount of structure in human-generated text, and if you have enough data and enough compute, you can extract that structure and reproduce it. That's impressive engineering. It's not the same as learning from experience.

The core thing I care about, and have cared about for forty years, is an agent that has goals, that acts in the world, that sees the consequences of its actions, and that learns from those consequences. Large language models don't do that in their basic form. They predict what a person would say next. They don't have a goal in the sense of a reward they're trying to maximize through interaction with an environment. They don't have ground truth. If I ask a model something and it tells me an answer, there's nothing in the system that finds out whether the answer was right and updates on that. It's imitation, not learning in the way I mean it.

So you could say I was surprised that imitation got this far, and not surprised that it has the limitations it has. It's a dead end in the sense that the data runs out. Human text is finite. Experience is not. An agent interacting with the world generates its own data forever, and that data is about what actually happens, not about what people have said happens.

I'll also say, and this is maybe the more interesting surprise, is how much of the field has rushed to treat this as the path. I'd thought the lesson of the bitter lesson was understood, that general methods leveraging computation beat methods built on human knowledge. And then we got a method that is entirely built on human knowledge, just scaled up, and people called it vindication. I'd see it the other way. It's a very big prior. It's the biggest prior anyone has ever built. But a prior isn't an agent, and I think the next real step will come from systems that learn continually, during their lifetime, from what they do. That's where I'd put my attention.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it was surprised by how well large language models work, specifically their fluent and broadly capable language performance.

astra-6.text:
The biggest surprise to me is how much you can get from predicting the next word. I wouldn’t have expected that objective, applied at sufficient scale, to produce such a broad range of capabilities. It’s a striking demonstration of how far learning from data can take you.

But I distinguish that from learning through interaction with the world. A language model is largely learning from the traces of other people’s experience. What I’m most interested in is the next step: systems that act, observe the consequences, and continually learn from their own experience. The success of language models makes that prospect more exciting, but it doesn’t make the distinction go away.

r001.rationale: The response says it is surprised by how much capability language models can gain from next-word prediction at scale, conveying that their effectiveness on language tasks was unexpected.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the biggest surprise has been how much you can get from predicting the next word. I wouldn’t have expected that to produce such a broad range of capabilities, or for the results to be as coherent and useful as they are.

But I would distinguish that from the question of how we get to intelligence that learns continually from its own experience. A language model learns a great deal during training, and then, for the most part, that learning stops. It can use what’s in its context, but that’s different from an agent going out into the world, taking actions, and getting better over its lifetime.

So I’m impressed by what’s been achieved. The question that interests me is how we move from learning from all this human-produced text to learning from experience.

r001.rationale: The response says it was unexpected that next-word prediction in language models could produce broad, coherent, useful capabilities.
